verses.2:1: Por que {fremuerunt} as nações: * e os povos meditaram coisas vãs?
verses.2:2: {astiterunt} os reis da terra, e os príncipes {inunum} * contra o Senhor, e contra o seu {christum}.
verses.2:3: {v3open} as {vincula} deles: * e {proiciamus} de nós o seu jugo.{v3close}
verses.2:4: Aquele que habita nos céus rirá deles: * e o Senhor {subsannabit} deles.
verses.2:5: Então lhes falará na sua ira, * e no seu furor os {conturbabit}.
verses.2:6: Eu, porém, {constitutus} sobre Sião, o seu monte santo, * {praedicans} o seu {praeceptum}.
verses.2:10: E agora, reis, entendei: * {erudimini}, vós que julgais a terra.
verses.2:13: Quando {inbrevi} se inflamar a sua ira: * bem-aventurados todos os que confiam nele.

decisions.latin: Fílius meus es tu … Póstula a me, et dabo tibi … Reges eos … confrínges eos
decisions.why: The psalter's first case of a divine person being spoken to — but by God, not by the one who prays. D1 makes God 'vós' when he is addressed; rule 3 makes a singular human addressee 'tu'. The Anointed of this psalm is, for the Church that prays it, the Son; so which rule governs? The question returns wherever God speaks to his king or Christ (109:1 Sede a dextris meis, 109:4 Tu es sacérdos in ætérnum, 88:27–28), and is distinct from the psalmist addressing the Messiah-king (Ps 44), which this does not settle.

options.label: tu

forms.pede: Pede-me, e eu te darei as nações como tua herança
forms.v9: Tu os {reges} com {virga}, * e como vaso de oleiro os {confringes}.

options.note: Ruling. 'Vós' in this psalter is not a mark of the addressee's rank but the voice of the one who prays: it is how a creature speaks up to God (vos-tu.md, D1). Here the direction is the other way — the Father speaks to the Son, a king is installed by his God — and the speaker owes no deference: a father who said 'Vós sois meu filho' would be keeping his son at a distance at the very moment the Latin is most intimate (Fílius meus es tu, ego hódie génui te). So the rule proposed for the glossary: address follows the speaker — whoever prays to God says 'vós'; when God speaks to a single addressee (his Anointed, the king, the just man of Ps 90:9–13, already 'tu') he says 'tu'. Both Portuguese antecedents have 'Tu és meu filho' here (Matos Soares 1932; DM1962 — who say 'tu' throughout, so this proves only that the line is known so). It also keeps the verse clear of rule 3: the 'vós' imperative of Póstula would be 'Pedi-me', which is also 'I asked'. The stylist named 2:7 the best line of the psalm, and neither blind reader was troubled by 'tu' inside a 'vós' psalter.

options.label: vós

forms.pede: Pedi-me, e eu vos darei as nações como vossa herança
forms.v9: Vós os {reges_vos} com {virga}, * e como vaso de oleiro os {confringes_vos}.

options.note: If the rule were 'every divine person is vós, whoever speaks'. Consistent on paper; in the mouth it turns the Father's word to the Son into court speech, and 'Pedi-me' stands only by D13's enclitic exception. Kept selectable so that Gustavo can hear it.

decisions.latin: Fílius meus es tu, ego hódie génui te
decisions.why: One of the best-known lines of the psalter (the Latin is sung at Christmas). The Latin puts the predicate first and the two pronouns back to back at the caesura: … es tu, ego hódie …. D2 gives order to the ear. 'Filho' takes the capital the DO Latin gives the other titles of the same person in this psalm (Christum 2:2, Rex 2:6; Fílius is capital there too, though it also opens the quotation). No article before 'meu': a predicate noun of kinship takes none even in article-keeping Portuguese ('tu és meu filho').

options.label: Tu és meu Filho, eu hoje te gerei
options.note: Ruling. The natural order, and the wording of both Portuguese antecedents (Matos Soares 1932 'Tu és meu filho, eu gerei-te hoje'; DM1962 'Tu és meu filho, eu hoje te gerei' — the second colon is word for word DM1962's, which keeps the Latin's ego hódie génui te in order). The contrast tu / eu still opens the two halves.

options.label: Meu Filho és tu, eu hoje te gerei
options.note: The Latin's order: the predicate first, and 'tu, eu' back to back as 'tu, ego' are. Solemn and perfectly sayable; less familiar to the ear that knows the line.

decisions.why: præcéptum is `open` in the glossary, proposed as 'decreto' by the Ps 118 study (words/ps118-terms.md §5) so that 'preceitos' could go to justificatiónes (D15). This is the first verse to meet it. It occurs 8 times, always singular (words/praeceptum.concordance.md), πρόσταγμα in six; here the Greek is τὸ πρόσταγμα κυρίου, 'the decree of the Lord' (the Latin has ejus, which is followed), and the decree is then quoted: 'The Lord said to me: Thou art my Son'. Douay-Rheims has 'commandment', Matos Soares 1932 'lei' — each a word the glossary has given to another Latin term (mandáta, lex).

options.label: decreto
options.note: Ruling: 'decreto' holds. Here it is exactly right — a king set on Sion proclaims a decree, and what follows is its text; the Ps 118 study's worry that 'decreto' is 'an act of government in Brazil' is here the point. Tried in the other seven places from the concordance: 7:7b 'no decreto que ordenastes'; 18:9 'o decreto do Senhor é luminoso' (the one ἐντολή, and the least natural — 'preceito' would sit better there, but it is sayable); 80:5 'Porque é um decreto em Israel'; 93:20 'que forjas o trabalho no decreto'; 98:7 'e o decreto que lhes deu'; 104:10 'estabeleceu-o para Jacó como decreto'; 148:6 'pôs um decreto, e não passará'. It fails nowhere. (DM1962 also has 'o decreto do Senhor' here — from the Hebrew, so it shows only that the word is prayable.)

options.label: preceito
options.note: The cognate. Would collide with justificatiónes → preceitos (D15), and 'proclamar um preceito' is weaker than the verse: a precept is taught, a decree is proclaimed.

options.label: mandamento
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'commandment'. It is mandátum's word (D15).

decisions.why: prædicáre is 'to proclaim publicly' (διαγγέλλων, announcing abroad). Its Portuguese descendant 'pregar' has narrowed to preaching a sermon (and is also 'to nail'). The participle hangs on the 'I' of the verse: I was set up as King … proclaiming.

options.label: proclamando
options.note: Ruling. What prædicáre means, and the gerund keeps the Latin's participle, with its openness (proclaiming as I am installed / in order to proclaim). Matos Soares 1932 resolves it into purpose ('para pregar').

options.label: pregando
options.note: The cognate (Matos Soares 1932 'pregar', Douay-Rheims 'preaching'). Today a king who 'prega' is giving a sermon.

options.label: anunciando
options.note: Plain and good; kept free for annuntiáre, which the psalter has some forty times.

decisions.why: The Latin follows the Greek (κατεστάθην … ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ): the Anointed speaks — 'I have been set up as King by him' — where the Hebrew has God speaking ('I have set my king'; so DM1962). Rule 1: the Latin's speaker is kept, and no turn is marked that the Latin does not mark. The glossary has constitúere → estabelecer (working, Ps 4:10).

options.label: fui estabelecido Rei por ele
options.note: Draft 2. The glossary's verb, in the Latin's own order (constitútus sum Rex ab eo). Draft 1 had 'fui por ele estabelecido Rei'; the stylist named it the worst line of the psalm — the inserted agent 'retarda o verbo e dá à proclamação um tom administrativo' — and the order is the ear's (D2). His verb, 'fui feito Rei', is the option below.

options.label: fui por ele estabelecido Rei
options.note: Draft 1: the agent before the participle so that 'Rei sobre Sião' was not broken up. Heavy.

options.label: fui feito Rei por ele
options.note: Stylist. Shortest and plainest; but 'fazer' is fácere's verb — the psalter's 'factus est' is 'fazer-se' in the glossary — and constitúere is to set up, to install, which is the picture on the mountain. Refused as the text, D2: another word.

options.label: fui constituído Rei por ele
options.note: The cognate, and the idiom ('constituir alguém rei'); Matos Soares 1932. If the glossary row for constitúere is ever reopened, this verse is the argument for the cognate.

decisions.why: The Latin does not translate the Greek χριστός but borrows it; a Latin reader hears 'Christ', not 'anointed' (which would be unctus). DO's Latin prints it with a capital. The word recurs about ten times (17:51, 19:7, 27:8, 83:10, 88:39, 88:52, 131:10, 131:17 and the plural 104:15 Nolíte tángere christos meos).

options.label: Cristo
options.note: Ruling: translate the Latin as Latin (rule 1). 'Contra o Senhor, e contra o seu Cristo' is what the column beside it says and what Douay-Rheims, Matos Soares 1932 and even DM1962 (from the Hebrew) print. Glossary: open, because the plural of 104:15 cannot be 'os meus cristos' and will need 'ungidos' at least there.

options.label: Ungido
options.note: What the word means, and it serves David and the plural of 104:15 without strain; but it un-says the name the Latin says, in the one psalm where the Church most wants to hear it (Acts 4 quotes this verse of Christ).

decisions.why: frémere is a noise before it is a feeling: to roar, growl, rage (L&S); the Greek ἐφρύαξαν is the snorting of horses. Douay-Rheims 'raged' and Matos Soares 1932 'se embraveceram' give the feeling; the Latin gives the sound. The verb comes once more, 111:10 (déntibus suis fremet).

options.label: bramiram
options.note: Ruling. 'Bramir' is the roar of the sea, of a bull, of a crowd — sound and fury in one verb, as frémere is; three syllables, the colon matches the Latin's eight. The ambiguity reader listed it as a word a hearer may not know; the stylist passed it. One reader, not two, so it stays (as átrio and exultação did); the plain fall-back is the next option.

options.label: se enfureceram
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'raged'; Matos Soares 1932 'se embraveceram'. The feeling without the noise; plainer.

options.label: fremiram
options.note: The cognate exists in Portuguese, but is rare and leans to 'quivered'.

options.label: se agitaram
options.note: DM1962 ('se agitam'), from the Hebrew's 'are in tumult'. Plain; neither roar nor rage.

decisions.why: ad-stáre: to stand up, take one's stand (παρέστησαν). 'Levantar-se' is the obvious verb, but the glossary already loads it with exsúrgere and insúrgere, both of which come in the very next psalm (3:2, 3:7).

options.label: Ergueram-se
options.note: Ruling. To rise to one's feet, to stand up against: what astitérunt says, in a plain verb that leaves 'levantar-se' alone. (The glossary has the transitive 'erguer' for extóllere — erguer as mãos; the reflexive is a different use.) Chosen over 'Puseram-se de pé' for length: the colon was +5 by the checker with it.

options.label: Puseram-se de pé
options.note: Goes with the glossary's stare → estar de pé; concrete — the kings get to their feet. Two syllables longer in the longest colon but one of the psalm.

options.label: Levantaram-se
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'stood up'. The plainest; a third Latin verb on one Portuguese one.

options.label: Sublevaram-se
options.note: Matos Soares 1932: says 'revolted', which the Latin verb leaves to the second colon (advérsus).

decisions.why: in unum (ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, 'to the same place, together') comes six times (grep): 2:2, 47:5 (convenérunt in unum again, of kings again), 48:3, 70:10, 101:23 and the much-loved 132:1 habitáre fratres in unum. The Latin says two things — they came together, and into one — and a rendering should be able to serve all six.

options.label: se reuniram juntos
options.note: Draft 2, the Latinist's fix (minor): 'como um só' says unity of purpose, which in unum may suggest but does not state — it can be no more than 'together', which is what the Greek says. He is right, and 132:1 proves it (brothers dwelling 'together'). The Portuguese is as pleonastic as the Latin (con-venérunt in unum; Douay-Rheims 'met together'), and two syllables shorter than draft 1 in an overlong colon. Glossary: in unum → juntos (47:5 'se reuniram juntos', 132:1 'habitarem os irmãos juntos').

options.label: se reuniram como um só
options.note: Draft 1. Keeps the Latin's 'one' and is a living idiom; the Latinist: it makes explicit a unanimity the Latin only allows.

options.label: se uniram
options.note: One verb for the two Latin elements — 'unir-se' is literally to become one. Shortest and most natural; convenérunt is no longer heard.

options.label: se reuniram num só lugar
options.note: The Greek's literal sense; supplies a noun and runs long.

options.label: se coligaram
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Interprets (a league), and the 'one' is lost.

decisions.why: The rebels speak with no 'they said' in the Latin, and none is supplied (Matos Soares 1932 adds '(disseram)', DM1962 quotation marks). víncula are bonds, fetters; the phrase returns in 106:14 and in the much-prayed 115:7 Dirupísti víncula mea. eórum … ipsórum are varied in the Latin (one word in the Greek); 'deles … o seu' varies likewise: 'deles' comes first so that the plural owners are audible at once, which 'suas' alone would not make them, and 'o seu jugo' closes the verse so that three verses running do not end on 'deles' (2:4 has it twice, for the Latin's eos … eos).

options.label: cadeias
options.note: Ruling. The traditional word for bonds that are broken ('Rompestes as minhas cadeias', 115:7); concrete (rule 5).

options.label: laços
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. It is the glossary's word for láqueus, the snare (Ps 90:3).

options.label: grilhões
options.note: DM1962. Vivid; narrower than víncula (leg-irons), and oxytone.

decisions.why: proícere, the verb of Ps 1:4 (quem próicit ventus), one verse-pair later: Ps 1 ruled 'lançar (de)'.

options.label: lancemos para longe
options.note: Draft 2. The stylist heard 'lancemos de nós' as a construction carried over from the Latin and asked for 'atiremos para longe de nós'. Taken by half: 'para longe' is how Portuguese says the pro- of pro-ícere and the 'a nobis' together, and it brings the colon from −4 to the Latin's length; the verb stays 'lançar', so that the reader hears the verb of Ps 1:4 again, as in the Latin.

options.label: lancemos
options.note: Draft 1: 'lancemos de nós o seu jugo'. Word for word; four syllables short, and the stylist heard a calque.

options.label: atiremos para longe
options.note: The stylist's wording. Refused only for the verb: 'lançar' is as plain, and it is the one Ps 1:4 has.

options.label: sacudamos
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 and DM1962 ('sacudamos de nós o seu jugo'). The idiom for a yoke — one shakes it off; but it is another verb (excútere), and the link with 1:4 goes.

decisions.why: Two verbs of mockery in parallel, each with eos: irridére, to laugh at, and subsannáre (ἐκμυκτηρίζω, to turn up the nose at), a late and rare word that the psalter uses a handful of times (34:16, 43:14, 58:9, 79:7).

options.label: rirá deles … zombará deles
options.note: Ruling. Laughing, then mocking: the plain pair, 'deles … deles' for eos … eos. Matos Soares 1932 has 'zombará' for the first verb and 'escarnecerá' for the second.

options.label: rirá deles … escarnecerá deles
options.note: Matos Soares 1932's second verb. Stronger and rarer, as subsannáre is; five syllables, and illúdere / derídere will want words too.

decisions.why: conturbáre (ταράσσω) is frequent in the psalter — Ps 6 has it three times (conturbáta sunt ossa mea) — beside the simple turbáre. Douay-Rheims 'trouble'; Matos Soares 1932 'encherá de terror', which explains.

options.label: perturbará
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist ('conturbar exige reconhecimento de vocabulário literário'), and the ambiguity reader listed 'conturbará' among the words a hearer may not know: two readers, so it goes (the precedent of opróbrio in Ps 118). The plainer of two faithful words (D2). Cost: turbáre and conturbáre will share a verb — they are one verb in the Greek (ταράσσω). Glossary: conturbáre → perturbar, to be tried on Ps 6.

options.label: conturbará
options.note: Draft 1. The cognate; would leave 'perturbar' for turbáre. Failed both blind readers as literary.

options.label: aterrará
options.note: Matos Soares 1932's sense ('encherá de terror'; DM1962 'espantará'). Narrows disorder to fear.

decisions.why: The psalter has both fines terræ (four times: 21:28, 66:8, 97:3 …) and términi (here; 71:8 ad términos orbis terrárum). 'Confins da terra' is the natural phrase, and it is fines' own cognate.

options.label: limites
options.note: Ruling. Keeps 'confins' free for fines terræ; plain and paroxytone.

options.label: confins
options.note: DM1962 'os confins da terra'. The phrase everyone knows; spends fines' word.

options.label: extremidades
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('até às extremidades da terra'; Douay-Rheims 'utmost parts'). Five syllables.

decisions.why: The Latin follows the Greek ποιμανεῖς ('thou shalt shepherd / rule') where the Hebrew has 'break' — the reading the Apocalypse quotes. Rule 1: 'rule' is kept. The same verb is in 22:1 Dóminus regit me and 79:2 Qui regis Israël. 'in virga' is instrumental; 'reger em vara' is not Portuguese, so the preposition yields (D2).

options.label: regerás
options.note: Ruling. The cognate, which in Portuguese still has the shepherd's and the conductor's sense of guiding as well as ruling. The subject pronoun is supplied ('Tu os regerás') so as to avoid the mesóclise 'Regê-los-ás' (rule 5).

options.label: governarás
options.note: Matos Soares 1932; Douay-Rheims 'rule'. Plain; it is gubernáre's word and has nothing of the shepherd.

decisions.why: virga is a rod — the shepherd's (22:4 virga tua et báculus tuus), the king's (44:7 virga regni tui), the chastiser's (88:33). One word must serve them all.

options.label: vara de ferro
options.note: Ruling, with Matos Soares 1932 ('com uma vara de ferro'). The concrete word (rule 5); without the article, as the Latin.

options.label: cetro de ferro
options.note: DM1962 ('Com um cetro de ferro'). Interprets the rod as the royal one only; 22:4 could not follow.

decisions.why: con-fríngere: to break in pieces, shatter (Douay-Rheims 'break them in pieces'); some ten places (45:10, 47:8, 106:16, 109:5–6 …).

options.label: quebrarás
options.note: Ruling: the plainer of two faithful words, and what one does to a pot; Matos Soares 1932 and DM1962. The verse closes on it, oxytone.

options.label: despedaçarás
options.note: Carries the con- ('in pieces'). Five syllables; keep in mind if frángere and confríngere ever need to be told apart.

decisions.why: A passive imperative: 'be instructed' (παιδεύθητε). The natural Portuguese, 'instruí-vos' (Matos Soares 1932, DM1962), falls under rule 3: 'instruí' is also 'I instructed', and here D13's enclitic exception does not help, because with '-vos' the first-person reading is a perfectly good sentence ('I instructed you').

options.label: deixai-vos instruir
options.note: Ruling. Keeps the passive sense (let yourselves be taught) and the verb instruir; 'deixai' is safe (past 'deixei'). Three syllables over the Latin.

options.label: sede instruídos
options.note: Word for word. In Portuguese it is heard as a state ('be educated men') rather than as something to undergo now.

options.label: recebei a instrução
options.note: Douay-Rheims 'receive instruction'. Safe ('recebi' ≠ 'recebei'); a noun for the verb.

options.label: instruí-vos
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 and DM1962. Refused under rule 3 (see above).

decisions.why: Rule 3 bites on a famous line: 'Servi ao Senhor' (Matos Soares 1932, DM1962) is also 'I served the Lord', and the object is a noun, so D13's enclitic exception does not apply. The same imperative opens 99:2 Servíte Dómino in lætítia. The Latin rhymes here on purpose or by grace (in timóre … cum tremóre), so 'temor … tremor' at mediant and final is the Latin's own echo and is kept (rule 5). 'in timóre' → 'no temor' ('viver no temor de Deus' is living Portuguese), 'cum tremóre' → 'com tremor': the Latin's two prepositions.

options.label: Sede servos do Senhor
options.note: Ruling, proposed for the glossary for servíre at the vós imperative. Keeps the root (servus → servo is in the glossary), is safe ('sede'), natural, and exactly the Latin's length. Cost: a noun and a copula for a verb, and the dative becomes a genitive.

options.label: Prestai serviço ao Senhor
options.note: Keeps the dative; 'prestar serviço' is the language of contracts.

options.label: Servi ao Senhor
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 and DM1962, and what the verse wants — and what both blind readers asked for: the Latinist (minor: 'substitui a ordem direta de servir pela formulação de uma condição de servo') and the stylist ('Sede servos pesa onde cabe o verbo direto'). Refused under rule 3 as it stands (D1, D13: the bare form) — the same position Ps 117:19 was in before D13, and it wants the same kind of ruling. If Gustavo ever relaxes the ban where a run of imperatives makes the mood unmistakable (entendei … deixai-vos instruir … servi … exultai), this is the first verse to give back.

decisions.why: exsultáre → exultar (glossary). Here with a dative, as often (80:2 Exsultáte Deo, 94:1 exsultémus Dómino): to exult 'to' or 'for' him (Douay-Rheims 'rejoice unto him').

options.label: para ele
options.note: Ruling, kept against the stylist. The dative as a dative; 'exultai' is safe under rule 3 (past 'exultei'). 'Cantai para ele' is ordinary Brazilian Portuguese, and 'exultai para ele' goes the same way. The construction is frequent, so this is a glossary proposal: exsultáre + dative → exultar para.

options.label: diante dele
options.note: Stylist: 'exultai para ele soa traduzido'. More native; but it is the phrase of in conspéctu ejus / coram eo — another relation (before him, not to him), so refused as the text under D2 and kept here.

options.label: nele
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 ('alegrai-vos nele'). Another case (in eo).

decisions.why: The Latin follows the Greek (δράξασθε παιδείας, 'lay hold of instruction'), not the Hebrew's 'kiss the son' (DM1962 'beijai-lhe os pés'). Rule 1. apprehéndere is to lay hold of, seize (L&S; also 'for complector, to embrace'); disciplína (παιδεία) is teaching and correction at once, and its cognate carries both.

options.label: Abraçai
options.note: Ruling, with both Vulgate-family versions (Douay-Rheims 'Embrace discipline', Matos Soares 1932 'Abraçai a boa doutrina'). 'Abraçar' a cause, a rule of life, is the living idiom for taking hold of it for good; safe under rule 3 (past 'abracei'). The grip becomes an embrace — L&S allows it.

options.label: Agarrai
options.note: The hand's grip, as in the Latin and the Greek; safe ('agarrei'). Rough in the mouth, and 'agarrar a disciplina' is not something one says.

decisions.latin: nequándo irascátur Dóminus, * et pereátis de via justa
decisions.why: nequándo ('lest at any time', μήποτε; eight times in the psalter) governs both verbs: lest the Lord be angry and you perish. Portuguese 'para que não' does not carry over an 'e', so either the negative is said twice or a frame is used that holds both verbs. irásci → irar-se, as in Ps 4:5. 'de via justa' → 'fora do caminho justo': 'perecer de' is not Portuguese; justa is an adjective and stays one (Matos Soares 1932 makes it 'da justiça').

options.label: para que o Senhor não se ire, * e não pereçais

forms.nequando: para que o Senhor não se ire, * e não pereçais

options.note: Ruling, with Matos Soares 1932. The second 'não' is the grammar Portuguese needs (D2); same frame as 90:12 'para que não'.

options.label: não aconteça que o Senhor se ire, * e pereçais

forms.nequando: não aconteça que o Senhor se ire, * e pereçais

options.note: Holds both verbs under one negative, as the Latin does, and the '-quando' is faintly heard in 'aconteça'. Heavier, three syllables over.

decisions.why: The rebels' words come with no 'they said' in the Latin. The ambiguity reader, hearing the Portuguese alone, took 2:3 for the reciter's own call to throw off the yoke of the kings — 'pois a mudança de voz não é anunciada' — and then heard 'o seu jugo' as the kings' yoke. A hearer of the Latin alone is in the same place: the turn is unmarked there too, and the psalm has three more such turns (2:6, 2:7b, 2:10), one of which — where the Lord's words end — the Latin leaves truly open.

options.label: no mark, as the Latin
options.note: Ruling. Nothing is supplied: no 'disseram' (Matos Soares 1932's gloss), no quotation marks (DM1962). The brief for this psalm is to keep every turn the Latin has and resolve none it leaves open; marking this turn would oblige the text to mark the others, and so to decide where the Lord stops speaking after 2:9. The one who prays the psalm daily learns its voices as the one who prays it in Latin does. The cost is the blind reader's first hearing, recorded here.

options.label: quotation marks
options.note: DM1962's way. Helps the eye, not the ear — the psalm is chanted — and only this turn is marked by this option; whoever picks it should decide 2:7b–9 as well.

decisions.why: The second colon hangs on the first colon's verb (dabo tibi), with the Latin's chiasm: gentes hereditátem tuam / possessiónem tuam términos terræ. Draft 1 kept the chiasm; the stylist found that 'a sucessão de tua posse e os limites obriga o ouvido a reconstruir a ligação com o verbo', and would repeat the verb.

options.label: e os limites da terra como tua posse

forms.v8b: e os {terminos} da terra como {tua} posse

options.note: Draft 2. The stylist's complaint answered by order alone (D2): the second colon now runs like the first — the thing given, then what it is given as — so the ear carries 'te darei' over without effort. No word is added and none dropped; the chiasm yields.

options.label: e como tua posse os limites da terra

forms.v8b: e como {tua} posse os {terminos} da terra

options.note: Draft 1: the Latin's chiasm.

options.label: e te darei como posse os limites da terra

forms.v8b: e {te} darei como posse os {terminos} da terra

options.note: The stylist's wording. Refused: it repeats a verb the Latin says once and drops tuam (D2).

decisions.why: The Latin rhymes at its two cadences — timóre / tremóre — and the Portuguese cognates do the same (temor / tremor). Rule 5 counts a rhyme at mediant and final a defect 'unless the Latin has the same echo'. The stylist, who does not see the Latin, asked for the two words to be kept but moved apart.

options.label: e exultai {ei} com tremor
options.note: Draft, kept. This is the case the exception in rule 5 was written for: the echo is the Latin's own, on the same two words, at the same two places, and the reader beside the Latin column hears it in both. Matos Soares 1932 keeps it too ('com temor … com tremor').

options.label: e com tremor exultai {ei}
options.note: Stylist. Removes the rhyme by order alone, and closes on 'dele' / 'ele'. One click if Gustavo prefers the ear's rule without the exception.

decisions.why: The Latinist's one major remark: 'de via' says separation from the way, 'fora do caminho' turns it into a place and 'resolve a expressão peculiar do latim'; his fix is the calque 'pereçais do caminho justo' (Douay-Rheims 'perish from the just way'). The Latin stands for the Greek ἀπολεῖσθε ἐξ ὁδοῦ δικαίας — perish / be lost out of the just way. períre stays 'perecer', because this verse answers 1:6 (iter impiórum períbit): the way and the perishing, in both psalms.

options.label: fora do caminho justo
options.note: Kept against the Latinist, and this is the one place where the final text stands against the gate (as D10 did in Ps 133). Reason: in Portuguese 'perecer de' names the cause of death — perecer de fome, de sede — so 'pereçais do caminho justo' would be heard as 'die of the just way', a wrong sense where 'fora do' is at worst a flattened one. 'Fora de' is 'out of', which is the Greek's ἐξ exactly, and it is Matos Soares 1932's wording ('não pereçais fora do caminho'), so it stays inside D2's outer bound. The blind ambiguity reader understood the colon at once.

options.label: do caminho justo
options.note: The Latinist's fix: the Latin's preposition and its strangeness. Misheard as cause ('perecer de').

options.label: longe do caminho justo
options.note: Says separation more clearly than 'fora do'; adds distance, which the Latin does not have.

decisions.latin: Cum exárserit in brevi ira ejus
decisions.why: in brevi (ἐν τάχει): in a short time — soon, or suddenly (Douay-Rheims 'in a short time'; Matos Soares 1932 'daqui a pouco'). exardéscere → inflamar-se (glossary, Ps 117:12). DO makes this a verse of its own, a 'when' clause followed by the macarism; the Latin's colon is kept between them.

options.label: em breve
options.note: Ruling. The cognate phrase; 'soon', with the Latin's shortness in it.

options.label: de repente
options.note: The other half of ἐν τάχει (suddenly). Resolves toward the Hebrew's sense.

choices.2:1: gentes → nações, pópuli → povos (glossary, Nunc dimittis). meditáti sunt → 'meditaram': the same verb as 1:2 (meditábitur), the link that joins the two psalms — the just man meditates on the law, the peoples meditate empty things. inánia → 'coisas vãs' (Douay-Rheims 'vain things', Matos Soares 1932), not 'vaidades', which is vánitas's word. The Latin's colon before the asterisk is kept inside the question. DM1962 has this psalm (monastic Prime); it was heard for diction only.
choices.2:2: 'advérsus … et advérsus' → 'contra … e contra', the repetition kept. First colon +1 by the checker in draft 2. The ambiguity reader asked whose Christ 'o seu Cristo' is — the Lord's or the kings': ejus is as open in form, and he heard the Lord's.
choices.2:3: No 'they said' and no quotation marks: the Latin has none (decision 'v3voice'). dirúmpere → romper. jugum → 'jugo' and 2:9 fíguli → 'oleiro' were listed by the ambiguity reader as words a hearer may not know: both are the Latin's concrete images and have no plainer name (rule 5).
choices.2:4: 'in cælis' plural → 'nos céus'. 'Qui hábitat' → 'Aquele que habita' (habitáre → habitar, Ps 90:1).
choices.2:5: ira → ira, furor → furor. The Latin's chiasm kept (falará … na sua ira / no seu furor … conturbará); 'lhes' for ad eos.
choices.2:6: 'Ego autem' → 'Eu, porém'. 'Rei' with the Latin's capital. 'super Sion montem sanctum ejus' → 'sobre Sião, o seu monte santo'. The speaker is the Anointed, as in the Latin and the Greek; nothing marks the turn but 'Eu, porém', as in the Latin — the ambiguity reader heard 'a king begins to speak of himself; who he is is not said', which is exactly the Latin's state. The article stays in 'o seu monte santo' (glossary) against the stylist's 'seu monte santo'. The first colon is the longest of the psalm (23 syllables in Latin, no flex): the stylist found it heavy for one breath, and nothing can be dropped from it.
choices.2:7: 'dixit ad me' → 'me disse' (Brazilian proclisis). The second colon is the Latin word for word: ego hódie génui te → 'eu hoje te gerei'.
choices.2:8: postuláre → pedir ('Pede-me'): the plain verb; pétere will share it. 'dabo tibi' → 'eu te darei': the pronoun supplied for the rhythm (Matos Soares 1932 does the same). The double accusative → 'como tua herança … como tua posse', without the article, which a predicate complement does not take. Draft 2 gives up the Latin's chiasm in the second colon for the ear (decision 'v8order').
choices.2:9: 'vas fíguli' → 'vaso de oleiro'. Both verbs of the verse keep the object before them where the Latin has it after; the verse closes on the verb.
choices.2:10: 'reges' → 'reis', bare vocative (no 'ó' unless the Latin has 'o'). intellégite → 'entendei': safe under rule 3 (past 'entendi'). 'qui judicátis' → 'vós que julgais'.
choices.2:11: See the decisions 'servite', 'ei' and 'v11b'. 'exultai' safe under rule 3. The ambiguity reader heard 'no temor' as fear of punishment before reverence, and 'com tremor' as bodily trembling: timor and tremor are no gentler.
choices.2:12: disciplína → disciplina: the ambiguity reader heard 'a regulated, obedient conduct' first, 'instruction and correction' second, 'punishment' third — the range of disciplína (παιδεία). períre → perecer (Ps 1:6). He also asked whether 'e não pereçais' is a second purpose or a new command: he heard the purpose, rightly.
choices.2:13: beáti → 'bem-aventurados', as ruled in Ps 1:1 — the two psalms are framed by the word. confídere in → confiar em (glossary, Ps 117:8). Both cola +3 by the checker: 'Quando‿em' and 'se‿inflamar' elide in the mouth, and 'bem-aventurados' is the price ruled on in Ps 1.

audit.note: Latin = DO Psalm2.txt, thirteen prayed verses, 2:1–2:13 (DO divides the Hebrew's v. 12 into 2:12 and 2:13), each with one '*' and no other mark. No titulus (D7). The Hetzenauer 1914 print read was skipped overnight and is owed.

Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps002.md. Vulgate-family support: Douay-Rheims and Matos Soares 1932 only (his Ps 2 sits inside the OCR span that runs from Ps 1 to Ps 3). The Diurnal Monástico 1962 has this psalm; it is from the Hebrew (God speaks in 2:6, 'beijai-lhe os pés' in 2:11–12) and was used for diction only. DO's Portuguese was not used as evidence (D12). Readings where the Latin goes with the Greek against the Hebrew, all kept: 2:6 the Anointed speaks (constitútus sum … ab eo) and 'prǽdicans præcéptum ejus' belongs to this verse; 2:9 Reges ('rule', not 'break'); 2:12 Apprehéndite disciplínam (not 'kiss the son') and 'de via justa'. Speakers: the rebels (2:3), the Anointed (2:6–7a), the Lord (2:7b–9), the psalmist (2:10–13) — no turn is marked that the Latin does not mark, and where the Lord's speech ends is left as open as in the Latin. Rule 3 checked at every vós imperative: entendei, deixai-vos, sede, exultai, abraçai are safe; 'instruí-vos' and 'Servi' were refused (decisions 'erudimini', 'servite'). Lewis & Short consulted for apprehéndo. Counts by grep over the DO Latin.

Draft 1: hard pass (ids and marks). Soft, accepted: 2:4 'deles / deles' and 2:11 'temor / tremor' flagged as rhyme — both are the Latin's own echoes (eos / eos; timóre / tremóre); 2:7 second colon −5 (the known line is simply shorter in Portuguese); 2:5 −3; 2:12 second colon +3, 2:13 both cola +3. Mended before the critics: 2:2 first colon +5 → +3 ('Ergueram-se' for 'Puseram-se de pé'); 2:3 / 2:4 neighbouring finals both 'deles' → 2:3 now closes on 'jugo'.

Draft 1. Three remarks: 2:2 minor (taken), 2:11 minor (refused: rule 3), 2:12 major (refused, kept as an option — the text stands against the gate there, with reasons). Everything else confirmed, the Septuagintal readings and every mark included.

outcomes.remark: 'como um só' makes explicit a unity of action that 'in unum' need not state → 'se reuniram juntos'
'Sede servos do Senhor' replaces the direct command with a condition → 'Servi ao Senhor'
outcomes.reason: Rule 3 (D1, D13): 'Servi ao Senhor' is also 'I served the Lord', and the object is a noun, so the enclitic exception does not apply. Wants a ruling; the imperative is one click away.

outcomes.remark: major: 'fora do caminho' turns the separation of 'de via' into a location → 'e não pereçais do caminho justo'
outcomes.reason: 'Perecer de' in Portuguese names the cause of death (perecer de fome): the calque would be heard as 'die of the just way'. 'Fora de' is 'out of' — the Greek's ἐξ — and is Matos Soares 1932's wording.

audit.note: Draft 1. Five verses remarked; best line 2:7 (Tu és meu Filho), worst 2:6. Taken: 2:5 'perturbará', 2:6 the order, 2:8 by order, 2:3 by half ('para longe', keeping 'lancemos'). Refused and kept as options: 2:6 'fui feito Rei', 2:8 the repeated verb, 2:11 all three parts ('Servi', 'diante dele', the rhyme moved).

outcomes.remark: 'lancemos de nós' sounds carried over from the Latin → 'atiremos para longe de nós o seu jugo'
outcomes.reason: 'para longe' taken; the verb stays 'lançar' for the link with Ps 1:4.

outcomes.remark: 'conturbará' is literary → 'os perturbará'
first colon heavy; 'fui por ele estabelecido' delays the verb and sounds administrative → 'fui feito Rei por ele sobre Sião, seu monte santo'
outcomes.reason: The order taken ('fui estabelecido Rei por ele'). 'feito' refused and kept as an option: it is fácere's verb. 'seu monte santo' without the article refused: glossary.

outcomes.remark: 'e como tua posse os limites da terra': the ear must rebuild the link to the verb → 'e te darei como posse os limites da terra'
outcomes.reason: Answered by order alone ('e os limites da terra como tua posse'); his wording, which repeats the verb and drops tuam, is kept as an option.

outcomes.remark: 'Sede servos' is heavy where the direct verb fits → 'Servi ao Senhor'
outcomes.reason: Rule 3, as for the Latinist's identical remark.

outcomes.remark: 'exultai para ele' sounds translated → 'exultai diante dele'
outcomes.reason: 'diante de' is in conspéctu / coram — another relation than the Latin's dative (D2).

outcomes.remark: 'temor' and 'tremor' rhyme at the two rests → move one: 'e com tremor exultai diante dele'
outcomes.reason: The Latin has the same echo on the same words at the same places (timóre / tremóre); rule 5 excepts exactly this.

audit.note: Draft 1, Portuguese only. Nineteen items, four unknown words (bramiram, jugo, conturbará, oleiro). One unknown word dropped with the stylist's agreement (conturbará); 'bramiram' kept with its fall-back as an option; 'jugo' and 'oleiro' are the Latin's images. The one serious finding is 2:3: the unmarked change of voice was heard as the reciter's own call — the Latin's own state, kept on purpose and made a decision ('v3voice'). The rest is the Latin's openness, nearly always heard the right way first.

outcomes.remark: 'meditaram coisas vãs': thought on worthless things / planned things that would fail
outcomes.reason: meditáti sunt inánia has both.

outcomes.remark: 'o seu Cristo': the Lord's, or the kings'
outcomes.reason: ejus is as open in form; the Lord's was heard.

outcomes.remark: the change of voice is not announced: heard as the reciter calling his hearers to break the kings' chains; hence 'o seu jugo' heard as the kings' yoke
outcomes.reason: The Latin does not mark the turn either, and marking it would oblige the text to mark — and so decide — the others; quotation marks kept as an option.

outcomes.remark: 'as cadeias deles': bonds imposed by them / prisons belonging to them
outcomes.reason: Bonds was heard first; 'cadeias' in the plural with 'romper' is not the jail.

outcomes.remark: 'na sua ira': his anger, or theirs
outcomes.reason: His was heard; sua follows the subject as in the Latin.

outcomes.remark: who is 'Eu' — the Christ, or the one reciting; whose mount; whose decree; who proclaims
outcomes.reason: Each is as open in the Latin (Ego autem … ejus … ejus … prǽdicans), and each was heard as the Latin is commonly read.

outcomes.remark: 'eu hoje te gerei': came into being that day / was that day declared Son
outcomes.reason: ego hódie génui te says no more and no less.

outcomes.remark: 'os limites da terra': the whole extent / the borderlands of a territory
outcomes.reason: The farthest places was heard first; términi has the same range.

outcomes.remark: 'os': the peoples, the territories, or the kings; 'vara de ferro' literal or figurative
outcomes.reason: eos is as open; the image is the Latin's and stays concrete (rule 5).

outcomes.remark: 'vós que julgais a terra': rulers who do justice / those who pass judgment on the world
outcomes.reason: judicátis terram has both; the first was heard.

outcomes.remark: 'no temor', 'com tremor': fear of punishment and bodily trembling before reverence
outcomes.reason: timor and tremor are the Latin's words and no gentler.

outcomes.remark: 'Abraçai a disciplina': instruction and correction / punishment / a regulated conduct
outcomes.reason: disciplína (παιδεία) has the whole range.

outcomes.remark: 'e não pereçais': a second purpose, or a new command
outcomes.reason: The purpose was heard, which is the Latin's construction.

outcomes.remark: 'em breve': soon / quickly
outcomes.reason: in brevi has both; 'soon' was heard.

audit.note: v2. Wording changed against draft 1 in five verses: 2:2 'se reuniram juntos' (Latinist; was 'como um só'); 2:3 'lancemos para longe de nós' (stylist, by half); 2:5 'os perturbará' (stylist and ambiguity reader; was 'conturbará'); 2:6 'fui estabelecido Rei por ele' (order); 2:8 'e os limites da terra como tua posse' (order). New decisions from the critics: v3voice, v8order, v11b, devia. Standing against a critic, each with its reasons in the decision: 2:11 'Sede servos do Senhor' (both critics want 'Servi', which rule 3 forbids — wants a ruling like D13) and 2:12 'fora do caminho justo' (the Latinist's major). Draft 1 is prayed.v1.json (flat text prayed.v1.vos.json, the file the v1 critics read). Owed: the Hetzenauer 1914 print read of the Latin.

Draft 2: hard pass (ids and marks). 2:2 first colon now +1 and 2:3 second colon now even (were +3 and −4). Soft flags left, all accepted as in draft 1: the Latin's own echoes in 2:4 (deles / deles = eos / eos) and 2:11 (temor / tremor = timóre / tremóre); 2:5 −3; 2:7 −5; 2:12 second colon +3; 2:13 both cola +3.

Draft 2 (prayed.vos.json), run because five verses changed. The 2:2 remark is gone; the two refused remarks are repeated word for word — 2:11 'Servi ao Senhor' (minor) and 2:12 'pereçais do caminho justo' (major). So the gate is NOT clean: it is clean on everything the revision touched, and stands open on two verses where the text is held on purpose — 2:11 by rule 3 (a ruling like D13 would close it), 2:12 because the calque says 'die of' in Portuguese. A third way for 2:12, not taken: 'e não vos percais do caminho justo' keeps the Latin's 'de' naturally (perder-se de), and períre does mean 'be lost' — but it would break períre → perecer and the answer this verse makes to 1:6 (iter impiórum períbit).

outcomes.remark: 'Sede servos do Senhor' paraphrases the command to serve → 'Servi ao Senhor'
outcomes.reason: Rule 3: the bare 'Servi' is also 'I served'. Wants the main session's ruling.

outcomes.remark: major, repeated: 'fora do' adds a location where the Latin has separation → 'e não pereçais do caminho justo'
outcomes.reason: 'Perecer de' names the cause of death in Portuguese; 'fora de' is the Greek's ἐξ and Matos Soares 1932's wording.
